Another important piece of information that might be pulled out from a metadata is about how a picture was edited. The Fotoforensics service seems to be the most useful here. A photo can be uploaded directly to the service, or a link option is available as well. First of all, FotoForensics shows the original and last modification date. But it also offers the ELA (Error Level Analysis) option. This is like a scanner that shows how the picture was manipulated, even though those changes aren’t visible at first glance. While having basic knowledge of how it works, it is possible to identify the scale and type of manipulation, such as photo montage, for example.

There are many recommendation materials and sample tasks about comprehensive photo analysis on the web. Here we name just a few of them:

– the same color areas under ELA should also be in similar brightness. If under ELA some area of the image is brighter than the other, it was possibly edited;

– each re-saving of a JPEG file compresses it with lower quality. On the hardly compressed image noise should be visible;

– an area that was placed from another image under ELA would be brighter than other areas. But brighter doesn’t necessarily mean edited, as sharpened areas also leave such traces (text, line, edge);

– photo editors such as Abode leave a rainbow trace on an image. These traces aren’t necessarily evidence of photomontage. It is enough to re-save an image with Abobe software to leave such traces.

Now, my kids are older (12 and 13 years old), so they fold all their own laundry and have done so for a few years now. I've been slowly teaching them how to wash their own laundry too, though that can be hit and miss - teenagers are not, as it turns out, as motivated to do chores as one might think. ;) However, when they were smaller, this is what I would do. As the laundry came out of the dryer, I sorted it into piles. One pile for each kid, one pile for Mr Sarcastatron's and my laundry, one pile for bath towels and bed linens, and one pile for kitchen linens. It is ten times easier to face a huge bunch of folding if you break it up into piles like this! Then it would get folded according to priority and time. If i was out of kitchen linens that would be the first pile folded. If one of my kids had no clean clothes their pile would be folded first. I would wait until they were napping to do it, or I would put on a t.v. show and let them veg in front of the screen for a bit while I folded, or I would wait until after they were both in bed for the night. Even now, I often fold our laundry in the evening while the mister and I watch a show together, putting all the folded stuff in piles on the couch before stacking it in the basket to carry upstairs and put away. But we still had weeks where the laundry would be piled in baskets waiting to be folded for days and days - hell, that is still an issue now! I have a basket of kitchen linens here in the living room that I meant to fold the day before yesterday.

Don't sweat it if you struggle to stay on top of things like this. There is only so much you can do on your own with toddlers in the house! And don't feel like you have to do it all at once. Chip away at it. Whenever you go in (or past!) the room where the pile is, make it your mission to fold ten or fifteen things really quickly and then put those few things away. It only takes a couple minutes at a time but it will make a difference as the day goes by.

When I finally have a working washer I'm going to try this method. Right now I'm going to my parents to was laundry bc our washing machine broke and I'm right where you are with baskets of clean laundry.

1 I have only 2 styles of socks from Costco, black and white. Sorting them is easy and when they wear out, they are easily replaced.

2 I have a cart on wheels instead of laundry baskets. It has 3 hanging cloth bins that I separate into blacks, white and colors. Each day everyone in the family sorts their clothes into the proper bins before going to bed. Jeans go into the colors but are pulled out and washed separately so as to not wear out other lighter fabrics and they can use up a full load themselves.

Anyhow, on laundry night (Friday) I throw in a load and do something for the 26 minutes (eat dinner) it takes to wash that load (whites or blacks first because they (in my house) are the clothes that dry the quickest. Throw the first load into the dryer and start washing the next. Now I have 1 hour for the dryer to finish. Vacuum the house for 45 mins and dust for 15. Pull out the first load from the dryer, replace it with the next clean wet load and then load in the 3rd load into the wash. Take the clean dry load and fold it on the couch, separating piles for each person. Finish dusting and tidy up the kitchen.

Remove the second load from the dryer and place the 3rd load into the dryer. Start the jeans in the wash. Fold the dry second load adding them to the piles on the couch and clean the washrooms and mirrors.

One more hour. Plan out your grocery shopping needs and meal plans for the week, if you have a dog, take them for a walk.

Put the Jeans into the dryer and start the towels in the wash. Fold and stack the 3rd load.

Spend an hour with your spouse, read something, or help the kids with homework. When the jeans are done, fold them and add them to the piles and throw the towels into the dryer. Don't worry about folding the towels tonight, get to that in the morning.

For the e tire process, get your kids to help. If they're old enough to walk, tell them you need their help and get them to transfer clothes from the basket to the washing machine, or hand them the wet clothes for them to put into the dryer. Teach them how to fold and sort clothes and then when it is all done, put away their clothes.

Saturday morning, pull off all sheets and pillow cases. Throw them in the wash and then fold and put away the towels that are in the dryer. East breakfast and plan out your day with your kids and spouse (or go over plans made the night before). After the sheets and pillow cases are in the dryer, head to the grocery store as soon as it opens. You will have fully stocked shelves, and if it is Costco, you can beat the crowds and be out of there in under 15 minutes of you have a list of what your're getting and stick to it.

Come home, put away groceries and the sheets should be dry by now. Make the beds. Now you have the rest of your weekend ahead of you while most people are still sleeping.
